title: Why the Wolves Never Finish the Moose

scenes.visual: Title card 'Why the Wolves Never Finish the Moose' over a flat cartoon of a snowy island in a blue lake, one moose and one wolf standing far apart. COLOUR MAP (both films): moose BROWN, wolves GREY, plant food (young trees) GREEN. A counter box sits in the top right corner in every scene after the title, white text on charcoal: 'moose per wolf: N'. Every island scene in this film is a made-up model, labelled 'model (schematic)' in the bottom left corner. All numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: If wolves eat moose, why don't the wolves eat every last moose? On one real island in Lake Superior, they never have. Let's find out why, starting with a model island.
scenes.visual: The question appears word by word as on-screen text. A real-looking map outline of Lake Superior slides in with one island highlighted, label 'Isle Royale'. Then the map fades into a simple cartoon island, label 'model (schematic)'. A big question mark hovers over a grey wolf looking at a brown moose.
scenes.narration: If wolves eat moose, why don't the wolves eat every last moose? On one real island in Lake Superior, they never have. Let's find out why, starting with a model island.

scenes.tts: First, two words. A population is all the members of one species living in one place. All the moose on our island make one population. All the wolves make another.
scenes.visual: On the cartoon island, a brown loop gathers every brown moose icon; label 'population: moose'. Then a grey loop gathers every grey wolf icon; label 'population: wolves'. The word 'population' stays at the top with its definition in small text: 'one species, one place'.
scenes.narration: First, two words. A population is all the members of one species living in one place. All the moose on our island make one population. All the wolves make another.

scenes.tts: A predator is an animal that catches and eats other animals. The animal it eats is its prey. Here, the wolves are the predators, and the moose are their prey.
scenes.visual: A grey wolf icon gets a label tag 'predator: catches and eats other animals'. A brown moose icon gets a tag 'prey: the animal that is eaten'. A wolf pack of three grey icons trots toward one brown moose, which turns to face them.
scenes.narration: A predator is an animal that catches and eats other animals. The animal it eats is its prey. Here, the wolves are the predators, and the moose are their prey.

scenes.tts: Moose eat young trees and other plants. Wolves eat moose. We draw arrows to show who eats whom. Each arrow points from the food to the eater.
scenes.visual: A three-step chain builds left to right: green young fir tree, brown moose, grey wolf. A thick arrow grows from the tree to the moose, then from the moose to the wolf. A small label under the arrows: 'arrow: from the food to the eater'.
scenes.narration: Moose eat young trees and other plants. Wolves eat moose. We draw arrows to show who eats whom. Each arrow points from the food to the eater.

scenes.tts: Now we need one number. Count the moose for each wolf. The counter in the corner keeps track. It is a rough clue to how easily wolves find food.
scenes.visual: The counter box in the top right lights up: 'moose per wolf'. Under it, a small on-screen formula: 'moose ÷ wolves'. Brown moose and grey wolf icons stay scattered across the island, NOT sorted into groups. On-screen arithmetic: '1,000 moose ÷ 10 wolves = 100 moose per wolf', with a small note under it: 'one number for the whole island, not each wolf's own share'.
scenes.narration: Now we need one number. Count the moose for each wolf. The counter in the corner keeps track. It is a rough clue to how easily wolves find food.

scenes.tts: Our model island starts with many moose and only a few wolves. The counter is high. In this model, that means hunting is easy, and the wolves eat well.
scenes.visual: Island scene with on-screen labels '1,000 moose' (many brown icons) and '10 wolves' (a few grey icons). Counter: 'moose per wolf: 100'. A wolf trots past full-bellied; green young trees dot the island.
scenes.narration: Our model island starts with many moose and only a few wolves. The counter is high. In this model, that means hunting is easy, and the wolves eat well.

scenes.tts: With plenty of food, more wolf pups survive and grow up. Year by year, there are more wolves. And more wolves catch more moose.
scenes.visual: A year label ticks forward: 'year 1, year 2, year 3'. Grey pup icons appear at a den and grow into adults; the wolf label climbs to '30 wolves'. Brown moose icons fade out one by one as wolves catch them.
scenes.narration: With plenty of food, more wolf pups survive and grow up. Year by year, there are more wolves. And more wolves catch more moose.

scenes.tts: So the moose population falls. Watch the counter drop. Now each wolf has only a few moose to hunt.
scenes.visual: Moose label falls to '300 moose'. Counter rolls down from 100 to 'moose per wolf: 10', turning from white to orange. The island now looks crowded with grey wolves and has scattered brown moose.
scenes.narration: So the moose population falls. Watch the counter drop. Now each wolf has only a few moose to hunt.

scenes.tts: Here is a question for you. There are now only ten moose for each wolf. What happens to the wolves next? Pause and predict.
scenes.visual: Question card over the island: 'Only 10 moose for each wolf. What happens to the wolves next?' The counter 'moose per wolf: 10' pulses in orange.
scenes.narration: Here is a question for you. There are now only ten moose for each wolf. What happens to the wolves next? Pause and predict.

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card holds; a 5-second ring timer fills at bottom right.

scenes.tts: In this model, that number is too low. Wolves catch too little food, and fewer pups survive. The wolf population falls. But look at the moose. Many moose are still alive.
scenes.visual: A small label appears under the counter: 'model rule: too few to feed the wolves'. Grey wolves search the snow and come back empty; a few wolf icons fade out. Wolf label falls to '12 wolves'. Then the camera pans across the island to show brown moose still browsing among the green trees, with a soft highlight ring around them: 'still alive'.
scenes.narration: In this model, that number is too low. Wolves catch too little food, and fewer pups survive. The wolf population falls. But look at the moose. Many moose are still alive.

scenes.tts: With fewer wolves hunting, more moose calves survive. The moose population grows again. The counter climbs back up, and the loop can start over.
scenes.visual: Small brown calf icons appear beside the moose and grow; moose label climbs. Counter climbs from 10 back upward, turning white again. A circular arrow forms around the island with four steps: 'many moose', 'wolves increase', 'fewer moose', 'wolves decrease'.
scenes.narration: With fewer wolves hunting, more moose calves survive. The moose population grows again. The counter climbs back up, and the loop can start over.

scenes.tts: This rule fits a predator that eats mostly one kind of prey. On an island, neither animal can easily leave. A predator with other food may not go hungry, and it could keep eating a prey down to nothing.
scenes.visual: The circular loop shrinks to the corner. A label box: 'fits: a predator that eats mostly one prey, on an island'. Beside it, a second small schematic: a grey predator with a bowl of other food (generic icons labelled 'other food') next to a few brown prey icons that fade out; label 'not hungry, so the rule does not hold'.
scenes.narration: This rule fits a predator that eats mostly one kind of prey. On an island, neither animal can easily leave. A predator with other food may not go hungry, and it could keep eating a prey down to nothing.

scenes.tts: A real island is messier. Weather, ticks and disease also change the counts. There, this number alone cannot show that wolves are hungry. You will see real counts in the second film.
scenes.visual: The model island gets real touches: a snowstorm icon labelled 'weather', a tiny tick icon on a moose labelled 'ticks', a germ icon labelled 'disease'. A small note appears: 'real island: the number alone cannot show hunger'. The 'model (schematic)' label stays in the corner.
scenes.narration: A real island is messier. Weather, ticks and disease also change the counts. There, this number alone cannot show that wolves are hungry. You will see real counts in the second film.

scenes.tts: So here is the answer to our question. When there are few moose for each wolf, wolves tend to catch moose less often. If they get too little food, fewer wolves survive. Wolves usually run short of food before the moose run out.
scenes.visual: The counter box grows to the centre of the screen and drops to a low number in orange; a hungry grey wolf sits beside it while brown moose stand in the background. The final sentence, 'Wolves usually run short of food before the moose run out.', appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: So here is the answer to our question. When there are few moose for each wolf, wolves tend to catch moose less often. If they get too little food, fewer wolves survive. Wolves usually run short of food before the moose run out.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex holding a small 'moose per wolf' counter. Line: 'Wolves usually run short of food before the moose run out.'
